summary: This informational memo explains how to use the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm with XML Signatures. It allows signing data of any kind to provide integrity and authentication, whether the data is inside the XML or referenced from it.

plainLanguage.summary: XML signatures let a program prove that a document has not changed since it was signed. RFC 4050 adds a third way to make such a signature, using elliptic curves instead of RSA or DSA, and defines the XML elements needed to carry the matching public key and the curve it belongs to.

questions: how to use elliptic curves in xml dsig
how to sign xml with ecdsa
why use elliptic curves for signatures
subtitle: How to sign XML with the elliptic curve signature algorithm, and how to carry the key in the document.

tldr.problem: The XML Signature standard defined only two ways to sign a document, RSA and DSA, and both produce large signatures and large keys. There was no way to use elliptic curves, which give the same security in less space.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adds ECDSA as a third signature method: a namespace, an algorithm identifier, a rule for turning the pair of signature numbers into text, and an XML element that carries the public key with its domain parameters.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo with an IESG note saying it was not reviewed by the IETF for security, so readers are told to exercise caution in evaluating it for implementation and deployment.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
RFC 4050 specifies how to use the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) with XML signatures as specified in RFC 3275. The XML Signature standard defines only two digital signature methods, RSA and DSA (DSS) signatures, and this document introduces ECDSA signatures as an additional method.

The mechanism provides integrity, message authentication, and/or signer authentication services for data of any type, whether the data is located within the XML that includes the signature or included by reference. The document uses both XML Schemas, which are normative, and DTDs, which are informative, to specify the corresponding XML structures.

The memo carries an IESG note. It says the document is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, that the IETF disclaims any knowledge of its fitness for any purpose, and in particular that it has not had IETF review for security, congestion control, or inappropriate interaction with deployed protocols. The RFC Editor has chosen to publish it at its discretion, and readers are told to exercise caution in evaluating its value for implementation and deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: When a program signs an XML document, it produces a value that anyone with the matching public key can check to confirm the document has not been altered. This memo describes how to do that with elliptic curves, and how to write the signer's public key into the document.

sections.title: ECDSA
sections.content:
The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is the elliptic curve analogue of the DSA signature method. It is defined in the ANSI X9.62 standard. Other compatible specifications include FIPS 186-2, IEEE 1363, IEEE 1363a, and SEC1. RFC 3279 describes ways to carry ECDSA keys in X.509 certificates, and FIPS 186-2, SEC2 and X9.62 provide recommended elliptic curve domain parameters for use with ECDSA.

Like DSA, ECDSA incorporates the use of a hash function. At the time of writing, the only hash function defined for use with ECDSA is the SHA-1 message digest algorithm.

The memo gives three reasons to prefer ECDSA. ECDSA signatures are smaller than RSA signatures of similar cryptographic strength. ECDSA public keys, and the certificates that carry them, are smaller than similar strength DSA keys, which improves communication efficiency. And on many platforms ECDSA operations can be computed faster than similar strength RSA or DSA operations. These advantages of signature size, bandwidth and computational efficiency may make ECDSA an attractive choice for XMLDSIG implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: ECDSA is the elliptic curve version of the DSA signature algorithm. It signs with the same idea, a hash of the data plus a private key, but the arithmetic happens on a curve. The result is a signature and a key that are both smaller than the RSA equivalents at the same strength.

sections.title: Signing, Namespaces and Identifiers
sections.content:
The specification makes no provision for an explicit version number in the syntax, and a future version would use a different namespace. The XML namespace URI that implementations MUST use is http://www.w3.org/2001/04/xmldsig-more#. Elements in the namespace of the XML Signature specification are marked by using the namespace prefix dsig throughout the rest of the document. The identifier for the ECDSA signature algorithm, as defined in RFC 4051, is http://www.w3.org/2001/04/xmldsig-more#ecdsa-sha1.

The XML Schema definitions in the memo are used with a preamble that declares the target namespace, the ecdsa prefix for it, the xs prefix for XML Schema, and version 0.2. The DTD form of the specification is informative. To include ECDSA in XML signature syntax, the following definition of the entity Key.ANY SHOULD replace the one in RFC 3275:

<!ENTITY % KeyValue.ANY '| ecdsa:ECDSAKeyValue'>

The input to the ECDSA algorithm is the canonicalized representation of the dsig:SignedInfo element as specified in section 3 of RFC 3275. The output of the ECDSA algorithm consists of a pair of integers usually referred to as the pair (r, s). The signature value, which is the text value of the dsig:SignatureValue element, consists of the base64 encoding of the concatenation of two octet streams that respectively result from the octet-encoding of the values r and s. That concatenation is described in section E3.1 of IEEE 1363.
sections.plainLanguage: The new material lives in its own XML namespace, so it never clashes with the existing signature elements, and the signature method has its own identifier, so a reader can tell which algorithm produced a signature. The signature itself is the two numbers r and s, written into the document as base64 text.

sections.title: Encoding the Key Value
sections.content:
The element ECDSAKeyValue is used for encoding ECDSA public keys. For use with XMLDSIG, it is placed inside dsig:KeyValue, alongside the predefined elements dsig:RSAKeyValue and dsig:DSAKeyValue. It consists of an optional subelement DomainParameters and the mandatory subelement PublicKey. If DomainParameters is missing, the application is expected to know it from other means.

Domain parameters can be encoded either explicitly, using the element ExplicitParams, or by reference, using the element NamedCurve. The latter consists of an attribute named URN bearing a uniform resource name as its value. For the named curves of standards such as X9.62, FIPS-186-2 or SEC2, the OIDs of these curves SHOULD be used in this attribute, for example URN="urn:oid:1.2.840.10045.3.1.1". The mechanism for encoding OIDs in URNs is shown in RFC 3061. The ExplicitParams element holds three subelements: FieldParams describes the underlying field, CurveParams describes the elliptic curve, and BasePointParams describes the base point of the curve.

The field parameters type is declared abstract and is extended by specialized types for prime field, characteristic two field, and odd characteristic extension field parameters. The prime field type holds the order of the prime field as its single subelement P. The characteristic two field type is itself abstract and is extended by specialized types for trinomial and pentanomial base fields; F2m Gaussian Normal Base fields are not supported by this specification, to relieve interoperability, and both specialized types share the element M, the extension degree of the field. The trinomial type adds the single element K, the integer k where x^m + x^k + 1 is the reduction polynomial. The pentanomial type adds the three elements K1, K2 and K3, the integers k1, k2 and k3 where x^m + x^k3 + x^k2 + x^k1 + 1 is the reduction polynomial. The odd characteristic extension field type holds M, the extension degree of the field m, and W, the integer w where x^m - w is the reduction polynomial.

The curve parameters type bears the elements A and B, the coefficients a and b of the elliptic curve, and the optional element Seed, which holds the value used to derive the coefficients of a randomly generated curve. The base point parameters type holds BasePoint, which represents the base point itself, Order, which gives the order of the base point, and optionally Cofactor, the cofactor of the base point.

The point type encodes a point on the elliptic curve as the subelements X and Y, its x and y coordinates. Point compression representation is not supported by this specification, for the sake of simple design, and the point at infinity is encoded by omitting both elements. The two subelements are of an abstract type extended by specialized types for prime field elements and characteristic two field elements. The prime field type carries a single attribute named Value whose value represents the field element as an integer. The characteristic two field type carries a single attribute named Value whose value represents the field element as an octet string, composed as shown in paragraph 2 of section 4.3.3 of X9.62. The odd characteristic extension field type carries a single attribute named Value representing the field element as an integer, composed as shown in section 5.3.3 of IEEE 1363a.
sections.plainLanguage: The public key element holds the coordinates of a point on the curve, and optionally the parameters of the curve itself. Those parameters can either be written out in full, or named, so that a reader can look up a standard curve. The memo writes out the full form as well, so that a document can be self-contained.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Implementers should ensure that appropriate security measures are in place when they deploy ECDSA within XMLDSIG. In particular, the security of ECDSA requires careful selection of both key sizes and elliptic curve domain parameters. Selection guidelines for these parameters, and some specific recommended curves that are considered safe, are provided in X9.62, FIPS-186-2 and SEC2. For further security discussion, the memo points to RFC 3275.
sections.plainLanguage: Using a curve is not enough on its own. The size of the key and the choice of curve have to be made carefully, using the guidelines in the standards the memo names, and the surrounding XML signature machinery has its own security discussion in RFC 3275.
